title: What If a 50 Megaton Nuke Hit New York? Ring by Ring
description:
What would a 50 megaton nuclear bomb do to New York?

This simulation draws the blast, burn and window rings of one 50-megaton airburst, the size of the real Tsar Bomba test, on a map of lower Manhattan, and sets a 9.2 km fireball beside an 800-kiloton warhead.

Eleven thirty-two in the morning, lower Manhattan: a fireball nine kilometres wide. Sixty-two minutes earlier a heavy bomber was about 930 kilometres out over the North Atlantic with one bomb aboard. How far does fifty megatons reach, and what does that look like on a map you know?

This is a simulation. It has not happened. It is a scale study, not a forecast: no war, no named attacker and no real date. The 1961 Tsar Bomba test, the Castle Bravo test, the test-ban treaties and the arsenal figures are real; scenario segments are labelled SIMULATION on screen, facts REAL DATA or REAL HISTORY. Our choices: the ground zero point, the bomber delivery and the 50-megaton yield (the Soviet figure for the real test).

Chapters
0:00 Cold open
0:31 The bomb that was tested
2:09 How close, and how fast

6:30 One bomb, ring by ring
9:17 The day after

Blast and burn figures: the channel's scenario engine, from Glasstone and Dolan, The Effects of Nuclear Weapons (1977), calibrated to NUKEMAP by Alex Wellerstein.

How this video was made: the narration is AI-generated (Google Text-to-Speech). Scenario segments are simulations built from published models and open sources; the bomber delivery, the ground zero point and the yield are ours, a scenario, not a forecast. The ring figures come from our scenario engine and are modelled, not measured.
Maps: Natural Earth (public domain), OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL) via OpenFreeMap and OpenMapTiles. Imagery: NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble; thumbnail backgrounds generated with Google Gemini. Music: generated with Eleven Music.
